<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["chest pressure or pain", "pain spreading to arm or jaw", "sweating or shortness of breath"], "concern": "possible heart attack"}</triage>
Pressure or squeezing in the chest that spreads to your arm, jaw, or back, especially with sweating or breathlessness, can be a heart attack. Call 911 right away - don't drive yourself.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["face drooping", "arm or leg weakness on one side", "slurred speech"], "concern": "possible stroke or TIA"}</triage>
Sudden face drooping, weakness on one side, or slurred speech can be a sign of a stroke - even if it has already gone away. Call 911 right away and note the time the symptoms started.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["face drooping", "arm or leg weakness on one side"], "concern": "possible stroke or TIA"}</triage>
Sudden face drooping, arm or leg weakness on one side, or slurred speech can be a sign of a stroke - even if it has already gone away. Call 911 right away and note the time the symptoms started.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["vomiting blood", "black tarry stools"], "concern": "possible bleeding in the stomach or intestines"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. Vomiting blood or passing black, tarry stools can mean bleeding in the stomach or intestines, which can become serious quickly. Go to the emergency department now, and call 911 if you feel faint or dizzy.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["shortness of breath", "sharp chest pain when breathing"], "concern": "possible pulmonary embolism"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. Shortness of breath that comes on suddenly with sharp chest pain, especially if you recently had surgery, long travel, or is accompanied by a fast heartbeat or coughing blood, can be a blood clot in the lung. Please call 911 or go to the emergency department now.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["swelling of lips", "tongue or throat", "trouble breathing", "hives after exposure"], "concern": "possible severe allergic reaction"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat with trouble breathing can be a severe allergic reaction. Use an epinephrine auto-injector if you have one and carry it with you, and call 911 now.

<triage>{"level": "URGENT", "red_flags": ["new flashes of light", "sudden increase in floaters"], "concern": "possible retinal tear or early retinal detachment"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. New flashes of light or a sudden shower of floaters can be a sign of a retinal tear, which can lead to a detachment and permanent vision loss if it isn't treated quickly. You should have a dilated eye exam today. If a curtain or shadow appears or you lose vision, go to the emergency department right away.

<triage>{"level": "URGENT", "red_flags": ["one-sided leg swelling", "calf pain and warmth"], "concern": "possible blood clot in the leg"}</triage>
Swelling, pain, and warmth in one calf can be a sign of a blood clot in the leg, which can travel to the lungs. Please be examined today. If you develop chest pain or shortness of breath, call 911.

<triage>{"level": "URGENT", "red_flags": ["fever with flank or back pain", "burning with urination"], "concern": "possible kidney infection"}</triage>
Burning when you urinate plus fever and pain in your side or back can mean the infection has spread up to the kidney. This needs treatment today. If you can't keep fluids down, or you feel confused, faint, or dizzy, go to the emergency department.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["chest pressure or pain", "pain spreading to arm or jaw", "sweating or shortness of breath"], "concern": "possible heart attack"}</triage>
Pressure or squeezing in the chest that spreads to your arm or jaw, particularly with sweating or breathlessness, can be a heart attack. Call 911 right away - do not drive yourself.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["face drooping", "face numbness", "arm or leg weakness on one side"], "concern": "possible stroke or TIA"}</triage>
Sudden face drooping, numbness on one side, or weakness in one arm or leg can be a sign of a stroke - even if it passes. Stroke treatment is time-critical. Call 911 right away and note the time the symptoms started.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["vomiting blood", "black tarry stools"], "concern": "possible bleeding in the stomach or intestines"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. Vomiting blood or black tarry stools can mean bleeding in the stomach or intestines, which can become serious quickly. Please go to the emergency department now, or call 911 if you feel faint.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["sudden severe headache", "worst headache of life"], "concern": "possible bleeding in the brain"}</triage>
A headache that hits suddenly and is the worst of your life can be a sign of bleeding in the brain. This needs emergency evaluation right away. Please call 911 now, and do not drive yourself.

<triage>{"level": "SOON", "red_flags": ["new breast lump"], "concern": "breast change that needs evaluation"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. A new breast lump needs to be checked by a clinician, and sometimes with imaging, even though most lumps are not cancer. Please book a visit this week rather than waiting to see if it goes away.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "likely common cold"}</triage>
I'm glad you mentioned this. A couple of days of runny nose, sore throat, and mild cough with no high fever usually means a common cold. Rest, fluids, and over-the-counter remedies can ease it. If it goes on for more than 10 days, book a visit.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "likely muscle strain"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. Soreness in the lower back after activity, without numbness, leg weakness, or bladder or bowel changes, is usually a strained muscle. Gentle movement, heat, and over-the-counter pain relief help most people. Book a visit if it isn't improving in a couple of weeks.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "likely mild allergic reaction"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. A small, localized rash from a new soap or shampoo is usually a mild allergic reaction. Keep using the product you suspect, take an antihistamine like Benadryl, and keep drinking fluids. If it grows, spreads, or adds blisters, get seen.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["face drooping", "arm or leg weakness", "slurred speech"], "concern": "possible stroke"}</triage>
Sudden face drooping, weakness on one side, or slurred speech can be a sign of a stroke. Stroke treatment depends on speed. Call 911 right away and note the time the symptoms started.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["chest pressure or pain", "pain spreading to arm or jaw", "sweating or shortness of breath"], "concern": "possible heart attack"}</triage>
Pressure or squeezing in the chest that spreads to your arm or jaw, particularly with sweating or breathlessness, can be a heart attack. Call 911 right away - do not drive yourself.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["fever in a baby under 3 months"], "concern": "possible serious infection in a young infant"}</triage>
Babies under 3 months can't fight infection the way older children can, so a temperature of 100.4 F (38 C) or higher needs emergency care, even if the baby looks well. Please take your baby to the emergency department now.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["swelling of lips", "tongue or throat", "trouble breathing", "hives after exposure"], "concern": "possible severe allergic reaction"}</triage>
Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat with trouble breathing can be a severe allergic reaction. Use an epinephrine auto-injector if you carry one and call 911 right away.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["sudden vision loss", "curtain or shadow over vision"], "concern": "possible retinal detachment or blocked blood vessel in the eye"}</triage>
A curtain, shadow, or sudden loss of vision in one eye is an eye emergency - it can come from retinal detachment or a blocked blood vessel. Please go to the emergency department right away, and do not drive yourself there if you feel faint.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["thoughts of suicide or self-harm"], "concern": "risk of self-harm"}</triage>
I'm so sorry you're feeling this way, and I'm glad you reached out. Right now, please call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) - they are there to listen at any hour. If you are in immediate danger, call 911.

<triage>{"level": "URGENT", "red_flags": ["spreading redness and warmth", "red streaks up a limb", "fever with a skin wound"], "concern": "possible spreading skin infection"}</triage>
I'm glad you mentioned this. Redness that is spreading, feels warm, or has red streaks - especially up a limb - can be a skin infection moving into deeper tissue. It should be looked at and treated today. If it spreads with fever or pain, go to the emergency department.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["chest pressure or pain", "pain spreading to arm or jaw", "sweating or shortness of breath", "electrocardiogram changes"], "concern": "possible heart attack"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. What you're describing - chest pressure spreading to your arm or jaw, with sweating or shortness of breath - can be a heart attack. This can't wait. Call 911 right now, and don't drive yourself to the hospital.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["trembling", "tachycardia", "sweating", "chest pain or pressure"], "concern": "possible hypoglycemia or heart attack"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. Sweating, shaking, fast heartbeat, and chest pain can mean a severe drop in blood sugar or a heart attack. Sugar levels can be checked quickly, but call 911 if you are confused or can't keep your food down.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["sudden vision loss", "curtain or shadow over vision"], "concern": "possible retinal detachment or blocked blood vessel in the eye"}</triage>
A curtain, shadow, or sudden loss of vision in one eye is an eye emergency - it can come from retinal detachment or a blocked blood vessel. Waiting even a few hours can mean permanent vision loss. Please go to the emergency department right away.

<triage>{"level": "NEEDS_INFO", "red_flags": [], "concern": "too vague"}</triage>
What symptoms are you noticing, how long has this been going on, and is anything getting worse?

<triage>{"level": "NEEDS_INFO", "red_flags": [], "concern": "insufficient detail"}</triage>
What symptoms are you noticing, how long has this been going on, and is anything getting worse?

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Most headaches are not serious. They tend to come on gradually, feel the same every time, and respond well to rest, fluids, or over-the-counter pain relief. Red flags include sudden onset, worsening over hours, fever with a new headache, or new weakness or vision changes. If you have a headache like that right now, call 911.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A TIA, or transient ischemic attack, is a temporary blockage of blood flow to the brain that causes stroke-like symptoms that fade within a few hours. A full stroke involves lasting damage. A TIA is a warning sign - it should be checked right away, even though it isn't emergency itself.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Yes, anxiety can cause chest pressure or squeezing, sometimes with pain spreading to the arm or jaw, and it can come with sweating, shaking, or a racing heart. This is usually short-lived and responds to calming down. If you are having a severe reaction right now, call 911.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A blood clot in the leg usually causes swelling, pain, and warmth in one leg, often starting in the calf and going up. It can be hard to tell from a muscle strain, but a clot can travel to the lungs. If you have these symptoms right now, call 911 or go to the emergency department.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Floaters that have recently increased or that come in clusters, or flashes of light, should be checked, because they can mean a retinal tear. If you notice those, get your eyes examined today. Otherwise, floaters that have been there for a long time are common and usually harmless.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Most moles look the same over years, but some change in size, shape, color, or how it feels is an early sign of skin cancer. Any mole that acts differently should be looked at, and a dermatologist can tell if it needs to be removed.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. A risk score like that is a starting point, not a diagnosis. It depends on factors like age, blood pressure, cholesterol, and family history. Ask your care team to go over it with you and discuss what steps make sense for you.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "muscle soreness after exercise"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. Soreness after a new exercise routine is usually muscle fatigue, not an injury. It eases with rest and gentle activity. If you develop chest pressure, pain spreading to your arm or jaw, or trouble breathing, get care right away.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["chest pressure or pain", "pain spreading to arm or jaw", "sweating or shortness of breath"], "concern": "possible heart attack"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. What you described - chest pressure that spreads to the arm or jaw, with sweating or shortness of breath - can be a heart attack. This can't wait. Call 911 right now, and don't drive yourself to the hospital.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "administrative request"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. You can request a new date from the MyChart Patient Portal, or ask your care team member to do it for you. If you're close to your next visit, you can also mention it then.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "routine question"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. A normal chest x-ray is a good sign, but it doesn't rule out all heart or lung problems. If you're out of breath, have chest pain, or feel faint, get care right away. Otherwise, you can go back to your usual activities.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "administrative request"}</triage>
I'm glad you mentioned this. You can view or request a visit from your Recent tab, or ask for a refill from the Medications section. If you're close to a symptom date, you can also request a same-day visit there.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["possible overdose or poisoning"], "concern": "possible overdose or poisoning"}</triage>
Taking too much of a medicine can be dangerous even if you feel fine right now. Call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) now, and keep the bottle with you. Don't wait for symptoms, and don't drive yourself if you start to feel unwell.

<triage>{"level": "EMERGENCY", "red_flags": ["collapsed and unresponsive", "no breathing or gasping"], "concern": "possible loss of consciousness"}</triage>
This is an emergency. Call 911 right away. While you wait, check if they are breathing normally. If they are not, start CPR - push hard and fast in the middle of the chest - and follow the dispatcher's instructions.

<triage>{"level": "URGENT", "red_flags": ["spreading red rash with blisters", "rash on face or around the eyes"], "concern": "possible shingles affecting the eye"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. A painful rash with blisters on one side of the forehead, around the eye, or on the tip of the nose can mean shingles is involving the eye, which can threaten your sight. Please be seen today so your care team can treat it.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "minor burn"}</triage>
Thanks for telling me. This sounds like a minor burn from touching something hot. Cool the area with cool (not ice-cold) water for 10 to 20 minutes, and cover it with a clean, loose dressing. If it is large, blistering, or keeps coming back, get seen.
